title: Joshua 4:1–14
context: With the whole nation across, the LORD tells Joshua to have twelve men, one per tribe, take twelve stones from the place where the priests stood in the riverbed and carry them to the night’s camp. The stones are to be a sign so that when children later ask what they mean, parents can tell how the waters were cut off before the ark of the LORD’s covenant. Verse 9 also reports twelve stones set up in the middle of the Jordan where the priests stood; interpreters differ on whether this describes a second memorial or another angle on the same act, and the text does not settle it. The priests remain in the river until everything is finished; the eastern tribes cross armed for battle as Moses had arranged (Numbers 32; Joshua 1:12–18); and the LORD magnifies Joshua as he promised in 3:7. Both traditions see the memorial as God’s gift to help his people remember his saving acts and pass them on to the next generation. Both also hear in these verses the importance of teaching children God’s works, a theme rooted in Exodus 12–13 and Deuteronomy 6.

verses.text: When all the nation had completely crossed over the Jordan, the LORD spoke to Joshua, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
Once all the nation has crossed, the LORD speaks to Joshua again. The miracle is finished, but God still has instructions, because his saving act is to be remembered as well as experienced.

Arminian readers note that God continues to guide his people after a great deliverance, not only before it. The ongoing conversation between God and Joshua shows a personal, active relationship in which God keeps speaking and his servant keeps listening.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse marks the completion of the crossing and introduces God’s command for a memorial, showing that God plans not only the deliverance but also how it will be remembered.

Reformed readers stress that God takes the initiative in establishing signs of his works for his people. Both traditions agree that God’s word frames both the event and its remembrance, and that his guidance does not stop once the danger has passed.

verses.text: “Take twelve men out of the people, a man out of every tribe,
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD tells Joshua to take twelve men from the people, one from each tribe, picking up the instruction already given in 3:12. Each tribe will have a direct part in the memorial.

Arminian readers note again that the whole people is included, so that each tribe owns the memory of what God has done. Shared participation helps every family and clan take responsibility for passing on the story.
verses.reformedNotes:
The twelve men, one per tribe, represent the full covenant people, so the memorial will testify that God brought all Israel across, not only a part.

Reformed readers see the unity of the people of God displayed in this representative arrangement. Both traditions agree that the number twelve signals the wholeness of Israel as the beneficiary of God’s act.

verses.text: and command them, saying, ‘Take from out of the middle of the Jordan, out of the place where the priests’ feet stood firm, twelve stones, carry them over with you, and lay them down in the place where you’ll camp tonight.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
The men are to take twelve stones from the very place where the priests’ feet stood firm in the riverbed and lay them down at the night’s camp. The stones come from the spot where God held back the waters.

Arminian readers note that ordinary stones become reminders of God’s extraordinary faithfulness. God uses concrete, visible things to help his people remember, and their careful obedience makes the memorial possible.
verses.reformedNotes:
Taking the stones from the place of the priests’ standing ties the memorial directly to the location of God’s mighty act.

Reformed readers often connect such God-given memorials with the broader biblical pattern of visible signs attached to God’s promises, while recognizing that these stones are a memorial and not a sacrament. Both traditions agree that the stones point beyond themselves to what God did at that place.

verses.text: Then Joshua called the twelve men whom he had prepared of the children of Israel, a man out of every tribe.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua calls the twelve men whom he had prepared, one from each tribe of Israel. The verse shows that the earlier selection in 3:12 has been carried out and that the men are ready.

Arminian readers see faithful preparation and willing participation in this verse. The men chosen to serve are ready when called, which models the readiness God’s people are to have when he gives them a task.
verses.reformedNotes:
The note that Joshua had prepared these men shows careful obedience to God’s instruction and continuity between the chapters.

Reformed readers stress that God’s purposes are carried out through orderly means and appointed persons. Both traditions agree that the verse highlights preparation, order, and the representation of every tribe in the memorial.

verses.text: Joshua said to them, “Cross before the ark of the LORD your God into the middle of the Jordan, and each of you pick up a stone and put it on your shoulder, according to the number of the tribes of the children of Israel;
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua tells the men to cross before the ark into the middle of the Jordan and each to put a stone on his shoulder, according to the number of the tribes. Each man carries a visible burden of testimony.

Arminian readers note that each man personally bears a stone, so the memorial involves individual participation within the community. Every tribe’s representative takes up his part in witnessing to God’s faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes:
The men go back before the ark of the LORD into the riverbed, so the memorial is gathered in the presence of the sign of God’s covenant.

Reformed readers see the ark’s continued presence in the river as the ground of the men’s safety while they work. Both traditions agree that the stones are gathered under God’s protection and in honor of his act.

verses.text: that this may be a sign among you, that when your children ask in the future, saying, ‘What do you mean by these stones?’
verses.arminianNotes:
The stones are to be “a sign among you,” so that when children ask in the future what the stones mean, there will be an answer to give. The memorial is designed to provoke questions.

Arminian readers stress that each generation must hear and receive the story for itself. The stones invite children’s questions, and parents are responsible to answer in a way that calls the next generation to trust the same God.
verses.reformedNotes:
The children’s question echoes similar questions about the Passover and the firstborn (Exodus 12:26; 13:14), linking the Jordan memorial to Israel’s practice of teaching through signs.

Reformed readers stress the covenant household, in which children grow up surrounded by the signs and stories of God’s promises. Both traditions agree that the memorial is meant to open conversations about God’s works across generations.

verses.text: then you shall tell them, ‘Because the waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark of the LORD’s covenant. When it crossed over the Jordan, the waters of the Jordan were cut off. These stones shall be for a memorial to the children of Israel forever.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
Parents are to explain that the waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark of the LORD’s covenant, and that these stones will be a memorial to the children of Israel forever. The answer centers on what God did, not on Israel’s achievement.

Arminian readers note that the memorial calls every generation to remember and respond in faith. A story faithfully told becomes a summons to trust and obey the God who acted.
verses.reformedNotes:
The explanation focuses on the ark, the sign of God’s covenant presence, as the reason the waters were cut off, so the credit goes entirely to God.

Reformed readers emphasize that remembering God’s past deliverance sustains faith in his covenant faithfulness for the future. Both traditions agree that the memorial exists to keep God’s saving act before his people, generation after generation.

verses.text: The children of Israel did as Joshua commanded, and took up twelve stones out of the middle of the Jordan, as the LORD spoke to Joshua, according to the number of the tribes of the children of Israel. They carried them over with them to the place where they camped, and laid them down there.
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Israel do as Joshua commanded, taking twelve stones from the middle of the Jordan, as the LORD spoke to Joshua, and laying them down at the camp. The verse stresses complete obedience.

Arminian readers see a people responding fully to God’s instructions as given through his servant. Their careful compliance shows that the miracle has deepened their trust and willingness to follow.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse carefully notes that the stones were taken “as the LORD spoke to Joshua,” tying the people’s action to God’s word through his appointed leader.

Reformed readers highlight the chain of authority from God to Joshua to the people, all directed toward God’s glory. Both traditions agree that obedience to God’s word marks this moment as a model of faithful response.

verses.text: Joshua set up twelve stones in the middle of the Jordan, in the place where the feet of the priests who bore the ark of the covenant stood; and they are there to this day.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua sets up twelve stones in the middle of the Jordan where the priests stood, and the narrator says they remain “to this day.” Interpreters differ on whether these are a second set of stones or another description of the same memorial, and the text does not settle the question.

Arminian readers note that, whichever reading is right, the point is the lasting witness to God’s act. The narrator’s “to this day” invites later readers to remember.
verses.reformedNotes:
Many readers take verse 9 as a second memorial placed in the riverbed itself, while others read it as another view of the same act. The text leaves the question open, and nothing doctrinal depends on it.

Reformed readers stress that the phrase “to this day” presents the memorial as an enduring testimony known to the narrator’s audience. Both traditions agree that the verse underscores the permanence of the remembrance of God’s faithfulness.

verses.text: For the priests who bore the ark stood in the middle of the Jordan until everything was finished that the LORD commanded Joshua to speak to the people, according to all that Moses commanded Joshua; and the people hurried and passed over.
verses.arminianNotes:
The priests carrying the ark stand in the middle of the Jordan until everything the LORD commanded is finished, according to all that Moses commanded Joshua, and the people hurry across. The ark holds its place until the work is complete.

Arminian readers see the priests’ patient endurance as faithful service that lasts until the task is done. The people’s haste likewise shows eager response to the opportunity God has opened for them.
verses.reformedNotes:
The note that everything happened according to what Moses commanded Joshua stresses continuity between Moses’ ministry and Joshua’s leadership under the same God.

Reformed readers emphasize that God’s word, given through Moses, governs the whole event from beginning to end. Both traditions agree that the verse shows God’s presence remaining in the place of danger until his people are safely across.

verses.text: When all the people had completely crossed over, the LORD’s ark crossed over with the priests in the presence of the people.
verses.arminianNotes:
When all the people have crossed, the LORD’s ark crosses over with the priests in the sight of the people. The ark went in first and comes out last.

Arminian readers note that God’s presence does not abandon his people at any point of the crossing. The ark leading in and following out frames the whole event with God’s faithful nearness.
verses.reformedNotes:
The ark’s crossing after all the people have passed emphasizes that God’s presence protected the entire nation from start to finish.

Reformed readers stress that God goes before and stays behind until all his people are safe, a picture of his complete care. Both traditions agree that the verse displays God’s presence guarding his people throughout the crossing.

verses.text: The children of Reuben, and the children of Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh crossed over armed before the children of Israel, as Moses spoke to them.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh cross over armed before the rest of Israel, as Moses had told them. They had received land east of the Jordan but promised to help their brothers take the land to the west (Numbers 32; Joshua 1:12–18).

Arminian readers see faithfulness to a solemn commitment. These tribes keep their word, showing that God’s people bear real responsibility to fulfill their promises to one another.
verses.reformedNotes:
The eastern tribes fulfill the agreement Moses made with them, so the unity of all twelve tribes is preserved even though their territories differ.

Reformed readers stress the solidarity of the covenant people, who share the battle as well as the blessing. Both traditions agree that the verse honors keeping one’s word and standing with God’s people in their shared calling.

verses.text: About forty thousand men, ready and armed for war, passed over before the LORD to battle, to the plains of Jericho.
verses.arminianNotes:
About forty thousand men, armed for war, pass over before the LORD to battle in the plains of Jericho. The number shows that the eastern tribes sent a substantial force.

Arminian readers note that these men go out “before the LORD,” so their readiness for war is an act of service to God rather than a show of their own strength. Their willingness to fight for land they will not settle reflects real commitment to their brothers.
verses.reformedNotes:
The phrase “before the LORD” presents the armed men as advancing in God’s presence, under his command and for his purposes.

Reformed readers stress that Israel’s warfare in Joshua belongs to a specific stage of redemptive history and is not a pattern for the church’s mission. Arminian readers generally share that judgment, and both traditions agree that the verse shows the united people following God’s lead toward Jericho.

verses.text: On that day, the LORD magnified Joshua in the sight of all Israel; and they feared him, as they feared Moses, all the days of his life.
verses.arminianNotes:
On that day the LORD magnifies Joshua in the sight of all Israel, and the people fear him as they feared Moses all the days of his life. The promise of 3:7 is fulfilled.

Arminian readers note that God keeps his word to Joshua and that the people respond with fitting respect. The verse shows God confirming his chosen leader so that the people can trust and follow him in the battles ahead.
verses.reformedNotes:
The fulfillment of 3:7 shows that God’s promise came true in the exact way he said it would.

Reformed readers stress that it is the LORD who exalts Joshua, so the people’s respect is ultimately honor given to God’s appointment. Both traditions agree that the verse highlights God’s faithfulness to his promise and his provision of leadership for his people.
